# Cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids as a cause of death: Characteristics, manner of deaths, trends, and their healthcare implications

**Authors:** Armiel Suriaga; Ruth M. Tappen; Elizabeth R. Aston; Lenny Chiang-Hanisko; David Newman

**Affiliations:** Christine E. Lynn College of Nursing, Florida Atlantic University | Center for Alcohol and Addiction Studies, Department of Behavioral & Social Sciences, Brown University School of Public Health

## Abstract

Cannabis remains one of the most widely used illicit substances globally, with 188 million users in 2017. In the United States, nearly fifty million people are reported to have used cannabis in 2020. As scientific and public interests in cannabis are growing, more research is needed to elucidate its safety and the death circumstances of people who use cannabis.

Retrospective study of all cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids as a cause of death in Florida between 2014 and 2020. The information included sociodemographic characteristics, cause of death, co-presence of other substances, and manner of deaths.

We used descriptive statistics to describe the characteristics of decedents who died with cannabinoids (CBs) and synthetic cannabinoids (SCs) as a cause of death using the Florida Department of Law Enforcement data from 2014 to 2020. A general linear model with repeated measures was used to examine CBs and SCs death rate trends.

A total of 386 decedents died from CBs (n=128) and SCs (n=258) as a cause of death in Florida between 2014–2020. The mean age was 41.14 (SD= 12.839). Most decedents were male (87.8%), non-Hispanic whites (65.3%), and nearly 28% of decedents were 45–54 years. While 100% of CBs decedents died in urban counties, 28.3% of decedents with SCs died in rural counties, among whom 39.9% were African Americans. Most decedents from CBs and SCs died from accidents (98.7%), with 12.57% cardiovascular-related illnesses involved.

Cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids as a cause of death pose a legitimate health problem to society. More people ages 45–54 died from CBs and SCs, affecting work-related productivity. Drug intoxications (from CBs and SCs) and motor vehicle collisions accounted for the majority of the accidents reported while under the influence of CBs and SCs. While most decedents from both CBs and SCs were non-Hispanic whites, a substantial proportion of African Americans died from SCs as a cause of death in rural counties. Despite the growing scientific interest in cannabis, the public should remain vigilant of the adverse health effects from CBs and SCs, particularly those with cardiac-related illnesses.

This study has clinical relevance to patient safety. In this article, our research team reported the cannabinoids (CBs) and synthetic cannabinoids (SCs) as a cause of death in Florida from 2014 to 2020, and their healthcare implications, including assessment, diagnostic challenges in detecting CBs and SCs, medical uses of cannabis and its adverse effects for public safety.

## Introduction

Cannabis or marijuana remains one of the most widely used drugs worldwide, with approximately 188 million users in 2017 (UNDOC, 2019). Eleven percent of Australians reported cannabis use in 2019 (Australian Institute on Health and Welfare, 2020), 5% of Canadians fifteen years and older used cannabis in 2017 (Government of Canada, 2021), while cannabis use among European adults 35–64 years old increased by 27%, with more than 20% of past-month users reporting high-risk use in 13 out of 26 countries in Europe (Manthey et al., 2021). In the United States, 49.6 million Americans twelve years old and above used cannabis in 2020 (SAMHSA, n.d.). As of May 2021, the number of medical cannabis patients in the U.S. has reached over 5.4 million (Marijuana Policy Project, 2021; Rosenthal & Pipitone, 2020). In Florida alone (where medical use of cannabis has been legal since 2014), there is a significant 965.66% increase in the number of people with medical cannabis cards, from 65,310 cardholders on January 5, 2018, to 695,986 cardholders as of March 18, 2022 (OMMU, 2018; OMMU, 2022).

Interestingly, this substantial surge in cannabis use is also reflected in the global sales of cannabis-related products, estimated to increase from $13.4 billion in 2020 to $33.6 billion in 2025 amidst the COVID-19 pandemic (Sanyal, 2021). While the growing scientific and public interests in cannabis continue to rise, there is a dearth of research about the death circumstances of people who use cannabis. Several studies related to cannabis were systematic reviews/meta-analyses, presented as case studies, or done outside the U.S. (Hartung et al., 2014, Gieron & Adamowicz, 2016; Angerer et al., 2017; Drummer, Gerostamoulos, & Woodford, 2019; Hvozdovich, Chronister, Logan, & Goldberger, 2020). This study is the first statewide analysis of cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids as a cause of death, including the trends in Florida’s CBs and SCs death rates.

In this article, our research team reported cannabinoids (CBs) and synthetic cannabinoids (SCs) as a cause of death (COD) in Florida from 2014 to 2020. Our study aimed to 1.) Examine the sociodemographic characteristics of people (all age groups) who died with CBs and SCs as a COD in Florida as determined by the medical examiners, from 2014 to 2020; 2.) Determine the presence of other substances and the health-related illnesses associated with CBs and SCs as a COD; 3.) Determine the manner of death of people who died with CBs and SCs as a COD, and 4.) Determine the trends of CBs and SCs death rates by counties and the data years (2014–2020). We also reviewed CBs and SCs, their sources, and routes of administration, including the clinical implications of CBs and SCs in light of these reported deaths from these substances. We use the term cannabis instead of marijuana (although these terms are used interchangeably). Also, we want to clarify that CBs and SCs are two different substances.

## Background:

### What are cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids?

Cannabinoids (CBs) are chemical substances found in the Cannabis sativa plant, popularly known as marijuana (National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, 2019). There are three main classes of cannabinoids, namely phytocannabinoids (plant-derived), endocannabinoids (endogenous ligands or naturally occurring molecules in the body), and synthetic cannabinoids (chemically engineered or manufactured) (Alves et al., 2020). While there are more than eighty cannabinoids (FDA, 2021), the main cannabinoids are cannabidiol (CBD) and delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) (NCCIH, 2019). The pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of cannabinoids may be complex, but once ingested in the body, they bind with the CB1 and CB2 receptors and exert their modulating effects (Lucas, Galettis, & Scheider, 2018). CB1 receptors are primarily located in the central nervous system but could also be present in the peripheral tissues and organs, while the CB2 receptors act mainly in the immune system and could also be present in the central nervous system (Kendall & Yudowski, 2017). Thus, CBs could affect the brain and produce unpleasant cognitive symptoms, including disordered thinking, memory, confusion, and coordination, and in higher dosage, exacerbate the symptoms of psychosis or schizophrenia (CDC, 2020). Cannabinoids can be ingested orally, smoked in hand-rolled cigarettes or pipe, vaped, brewed as tea, or mixed in edibles such as cookies, brownies, or gummies (NIDA, 2019).

The FDA reported that it is illegal to market CBD as a food supplement or add it to a food item (FDA, 2020b). There are common misconceptions about CBDs, i.e., non-psychoactive and non-psychotropic; thus, it is safe to use (Russo, 2017). Cannabidiol carries a substantial drug abuse liability (Russo, 2017). CBDs have the potential to cause harm such as liver injury, and when taken with other substances such as alcohol or other drugs used to treat anxiety sleep disorders, stress could lead to increased sedation and drowsiness, which in turn, increases a person’s risks for injuries (FDA, 2020). Meanwhile, THC is widely known to cause a high in people who use cannabis (NCCIH, 2019).

The potency of cannabinoids has also increased over the years; the CBD content in cannabis products had decreased from nearly .28% in 2001 to .015% in 2014, resulting in a higher THC concentration (ElSohly et al., 2016). Thus, increasing the risk for problematic cannabis use, particularly among young adults (National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine (2017). It should be noted that both CBs and SCs have been classified as schedule 1 drugs, meaning they have high abuse potential with no medical use. However, in December 2018, the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 or known as the 2018 Farm Bill, removed hemp from the Controlled Substances Act, meaning that the Cannabis sativa plant and its derivatives, including cannabinoids that contain no more than 0.3 % THC on a dry weight is “no longer included as controlled substances under federal law” (FDA, 2021).

Meanwhile, SCs are part of the new psychoactive substances (NPS) that are two to one hundred times more potent than tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) (Darke et al., 2021; Riederer et al., 2016). SCs are manufactured chemicals sprayed onto dried, shredded leaves or plant materials that mimic the effect of cannabis, but their actual effects are unpredictable, harmful, and deadly (NIDA, 2017). SC was initially developed to examine the endocannabinoid receptor pathways but later emerged as a drug of abuse (CDC, 2017). SC-containing products are sold in gas stations, on the internet, and in novelty shops under different names such as K2/Spice, Bliss, Black Mamba, Blaze, Bombay Blue, Fake Weed, Legal Weed, Genie, Dream, and Crazy Clown (US DEA, 2017).

The European Monitoring Center for Drugs and Drug Addiction (2017) identified 169 SCs. Alves et al. (2020) had presented several chemical classes of SCs such as naphthoylindoles which include JWH-015, JWH-018, JWH-019, JWH-030, and MAM 2201; phenylacetylindoles (JWH-250, JWH-251); naphthoylpyrroles (JWH-037); aminoalkylindoles (WIN55, 212–2, PB-22, 5F-22); tetramethylcyclo-propyl indoles (UR-144, XLR-11), indazole carboxamide (AB-FUBINACA, MDMB-FUBINACA, APINACA, AB-PINACA, AB-CHMINACA); pyrazole (AM-251), benzoylindoles (AM-679, AM-694), adamantylindoles (AM-1248) and cyclohexylphenols (CP47, 497, CP 55, 940). More than 450 SC compounds were synthesized (Alves et al., 2020). Several of these SCs bore the initials of those who synthetized them, such as JWH compounds which stand for John W. Huffman, HU-210 at Hebrew University (Fontanet et al., 2018; Alves et al., 2020). In addition, some SC analogs were named after the Japanese and the Korean bands such as AKB-48 and 2NE1 as alternates to their chemical names APINACA (N-(1-adamantyl)-1-pentyl-1H-indazole-3-carboxamide, and APICA (N-1-adamantyl)-1-pentyl-1H-indole-3-carboxamide (EMCDDA, 2017; Alves et al., 2020). Newer SCs emerged in the market, such as AB-PINACA, an aminocarbonyl indazole carboxamide with different chemical structures designed to circumvent the law (UNODC, 2022).

### Cannabis Risk Perception and Its Adverse Health Outcomes

One primary reason for the continued increase in cannabis use is risk perception. The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (2021) reported that a lower perception of drug risks such as cannabis was correlated with increased drug use. The percentage of adolescents who perceived cannabis as harmful decreased significantly by 40% in the U.S. from 1995 to 2019 and by a 25% decrease in Europe from 2002 to 2019 (UNODC, 2021). Concurrent with this reduction in risk perception about cannabis, the cannabis potency increased substantially over the years in the U.S., for instance, from 4% in 1995 to 12% in 2014 (ElSohly et al., 2016), thus making its effects more dangerous, particularly to long-term users with health-related consequences (UNODC, 2021; NIDA, 2020a).

Consequently, using cannabis comes with real risks, including death (SAMHSA, 2021). The Global Burden of Disease study reported that approximately 22.1 million people in the world had cannabis use disorder (95% Uncertainty Interval [UI] 19 – 25.9 million) (Degenhardt et al., 2018). About 13.1 million people worldwide had cannabis dependence in 2010 (Degenhardt et al., 2013). In a meta-analysis of people who used cannabis which was conducted between 2009 to 2019, 13% had cannabis dependence, 18% had cannabis abuse, and 22% had cannabis use disorder (Leung, Chan, Hides, and Hall, 2020). Cannabis use disorder is a problematic pattern of cannabis use where a person suffers a clinically significant impairment of at least two of the following symptoms, 1) a person takes a larger amount of cannabis, or longer, 2) has a persistent desire or unsuccessful efforts to cut down cannabis usage, 3) suffers from craving, 4) recurrent use of cannabis results in failure to do obligations at work, school or home, 5) persistently using cannabis despite interpersonal problems caused by its use, 6) continued use of cannabis in situations where it is physically hazardous, 7) continued cannabis use despite knowledge of having a persistent psychological or physiologic problem, 8) tolerance and 9) withdrawal (Patel & Marwaha, 2022). Moreover, the risk of developing cannabis dependence increased by 33% in people who used cannabis daily or weekly Leung et al., 2020). Fischer and colleagues (2015) reported rudimentary estimates of cannabis-related mortality and morbidity, particularly on vehicular motor accidents (VMA), cannabis use disorder, psychosis, and lung cancer. VMA and lung cancer were identified as the dominant domains of cannabis-attributable mortality (Fischer and colleagues, 2015).

The Drug Abuse Warning Network (DAWN) reported a 21% increase in emergency department visits of patients with cannabis-related diagnoses in the U.S. from 2009 to 2011 (NIDA, 2020b). The National Institute on Drug Abuse (2017) reported 28,531 emergency room visits related to synthetic cannabinoids in the US in 2011, and 78% of these ER visits involved adolescents and young adults 12 to 29 years old. There were clusters of adverse health effects associated with synthetic cannabinoid use reported in the U.S. from 2011 to 2015, including deaths (n=20) (Trecki, Gerona, & Schwartz, 2015).

## Methods

### Design

This is a retrospective study of people who died from CBs and SCs as a COD in Florida from 2014 to 2020. The Florida Atlantic University Institutional Review Board has approved this study.

### Data Source

Our research team analyzed de-identified data from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement from 2014 to 2020 titled Reports of Drugs Identified in Deceased Persons (FDLE, 2020). These FDLE reports are public records that contain raw data of deceased persons with drugs identified in the decedent’s body. There were 49 drugs or substances, not including analytes and metabolites belonging to the raw FDLE data, such as opioids, stimulants, ethanol, benzodiazepines, psychedelics, cannabinoids, and synthetic cannabinoids. There were 82,079 cases of deceased persons from 2014 to 2020. The FDLE started tracking drugs such as cocaine in 1987, and in 1995 added heroin, and eventually added several emerging drugs that have the potential for abuse, and as the drug prevalence becomes known to the medical examiners such as cannabinoids (FDLE, 2021). As a government source data, FDLE aims to provide critical data on drug deaths in Florida to benefit local and state governments in allocating resources and appropriate services (OPPAGA, n.d.). Yan & Weber (2019) reported that government source data are reliable and dependable for research.

The Florida Department of Law Enforcement (FDLE) (2021) medical examiners determined the substance as a cause of death only if the substance, such as CBs or SCs, played a causal role in the death of a person by examining all the evidence such as autopsy and toxicology reports. According to the FDLE annual reports (2021), a decedent might have multiple drugs listed as a cause of death, but after a thorough examination, the medical examiners would rule out these findings as drug occurrences and not primarily as a cause of death (FDLE, 2021).

### Process of Data Selection and Population Density

For this study, we purposely extracted data of decedents with CBs and SCs identified as a cause of death on the FDLE reports for analysis from 2014 to 2020. We excluded the cases where CBs (n= 16,085) and SCs (n= 63) were present at the time of death but not as a cause. There were 82,079 cases of deceased persons with drugs identified on the FDLE raw data from 2014 to 2020 including those decedents with opioids, benzodiazepines, hallucinogens, stimulants. All data under CBs and SCs identified as a COD on the FDLE reports were visually inspected by the authors, and each case was examined per year, starting from 2014 to 2020, for missing items such as sociodemographic variables of age, sex, race/ethnicity, and population density by counties. Fortunately, no missing items were observed on the FDLE raw data for CBs and SCs.

Also, the FDLE raw data contained the county for each deceased person, including the cause of death and the manner of death. We then classified each county in Florida (n=67) as an urban (metropolitan) or rural (nonmetropolitan) county. The purpose of classifying the counties into rural or urban counties was to track a trend of CBs and SCs as a COD in these counties. We classified the urban counties into the large central metro, large fringe metro, medium metro, small metro, and rural counties into micropolitan and noncore using the 2013 National Center for Health Statistics’ classification of counties (Ingram & Franco, 2014). This county classification is based on the Metro Statistical Area or MSA and other criteria. For instance, a large central metro has an MSA of one million or more population that contains the entire population of the largest city of the MSA or contains inhabitants of 250,000 of any principal city of the MSA. Large fringe metro is a county with an MSA of one million or more population that did not qualify as large central metro. The medium metro is urban counties with a 250,000–999,999 MSA population.

Meanwhile, the nonmetropolitan counties are subcategorized as micropolitan, centered on urban clusters of 10,000–49,999. The noncore counties are defined as nonmetro counties not included in the micropolitan counties. For a list of Florida counties by population density, see table 1.

The FDLE reports categorize the manner of death into five categories: accident, homicide, natural cause, suicide, and undetermined cause. The authors inspected the manner of death coding for appropriateness. In this study, accidents were operationally defined as drug intoxications identified by the medical examiners, motor vehicular collisions, accidental injury such as drowning, firework explosion, fall (National Safety Council, 2018). Homicide is the killing of a human being by another, a natural cause is death from natural agents such as an illness (i.e., cardiovascular disease, hypertension), suicide is the intentional killing of oneself such as by hanging, and the undetermined cause refers to an unknown cause of death. The co-presence of other substances such as stimulants, cocaine, heroin, opioids, was also included by quantifying the frequency of their occurrences and health-related illnesses reported here as clinical characteristics.

### Statistical Analysis

Descriptive statistics were used to describe the characteristics of people who died from CBs and SCs as a COD. A general linear model with repeated measures was used to examine the trends of CBs and SCs death rate as a COD. We selected the beginning time point in determining the CBs and SCs death rate trends, for instance, from 2014 to 2020 due to the data availability from FDLE (Ingram et al., 2018). Our selected threshold for statistical significance was .05.

In calculating the CBs and SCs death rate, we added the number of deaths from CBs and SCs as a COD respectively by Florida counties per year as identified on the FDLE reports. We used the following formula in calculating the death rate: # of deaths from CBs or SCs divided by the total population by Florida county x 100,000 (Divisha, n.d.). The population data by county were obtained from the US census bureau, and we used the data for 2020 (uscensus.gov/quickfacts/FL). All data were analyzed using SPSS 28.

## Results

### Decedent’s Characteristics

A total of 386 decedents out of 16,534 cases were identified with CBs and SCs as a cause of death in Florida from 2014 to 2020. The mean age was 41.14 (SD= 12.839), ranging from 0–74. More people died from SCs (n= 258) than CBs (n= 128) as a COD. The highest count of decedents with CBs as a COD was in 2019 (n=49). The highest count for SCs as a COD was in 2018 (n=86). The lowest count of deaths from CBs (n=1) and SCs (n= 3) occurred in 2014, respectively. The majority of people who died with these substances were male (87.8%), and more males died from SCs (92.2%) than CBs (78.9%). All CBs as a COD happened in the urban counties, while nearly 30% of SCs as a COD occurred in rural counties in Florida. While non-Hispanic whites were mostly affected, more blacks died from SCs as a COD (39.9%) than CBs (13.3%). An overwhelming proportion of CBs (99.2%) and SCs (98.4%) as a COD resulted in accidents, with a single suicide accounting for both substances. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, more decedents died from CBs as a COD (n=42) than SCs as a COD (n=37). Table 2 summarizes the sociodemographic differences of decedents with CBs and SCs as a COD.

### Clinical Characteristics

A notable portion of the decedents who died from CBs and SCs as a COD had cardiovascular-related health conditions at 12.9% (n=50), of which hypertensive heart disease had the most occurrences at nearly 6% (n=23), followed by atherosclerotic heart disease at 1.56% (n= 6). Cardiomegaly was present in 5 cases of SCs as a COD. Hypoxic encephalopathy was the most prevalent pulmonary-related health condition at 1.56% (n= 6), then chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or COPD at 1.29% (n= 5), followed by cardiopulmonary arrest with four cases decedents with SCs as a COD. Eighteen cases for both CBs and SCs involved pulmonary-related illnesses. Consequently, one case (0-year-old) involved complications from maternal premature rupture of membranes associated with the prolapsed umbilical cord, attributed to maternal drug abuse-- opiates, amphetamine, benzodiazepine, and CBs; and acute bacterial meningoencephalitis (n=1). For a list of health-related diagnoses associated with CBs and SCs as a COD in this study, see table 3.

### Toxicology

The most prevalent drug or substance associated with CBs as a COD was delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol or THC at 36.71% (n=47). No actual dose (mg) of THC content was reported for all cases (except one) on the FDLE reports, followed by fentanyl at 20.31% (n=26) and ethanol at 20.31% (n=26). The blood alcohol concentration listed on the FDLE report was limited. In 2015, one case reported a BAC at 213 mg/dL. For SCs as a cause of death, the most prevalent substances identified were 3-dimethyl-butanoic acid at 18.21% (n=47), followed by 3-methyl-butanoic acid at 7.75% (n=20), then ethanol at 6.2% (n=16), without the blood alcohol concentration reported on the FDLE raw data (except in 2015).

There were 29 chemical compounds identified for synthetic cannabinoids (see table 4). Of these SC chemical compounds identified, the most prevalent was 5F-ADB at 25.96% (n=67), then 5F-ADB-3 at 17.05% (n=44), followed by 5F- MDMB-PICA at 13.17% (n=34), and ADB-FUBINACA at 3.87% (n=10). 5F-MDMB-PICA was most prevalent in 2020, with 22 occurrences. XLR-11 and XLR-99 were identified in decedents in 2014.

Nearly thirty-six percent (n=46) of CBs as a COD involved cannabinoids as the sole drug identified, while nearly forty-seven percent (n=60) of CBs as a COD involved multiple drugs (more than two substances identified such as opiates, stimulants, heroin, cocaine, pseudoephedrine, and ethanol). Meanwhile, approximately sixty-five percent (n=167) of cases in SCs as a COD involved synthetic cannabinoid as the sole drug identified, and nearly twenty percent (n=51) of SCs as a COD involved multiple drugs. See table 3 for the presence of other drugs for both CBs and SCs as a COD.

### Manner of Death

An overwhelming number of deaths from CBs and SCs between 2014 and 2020 resulted in accidents (98.7%). Most of these accidents were due to drug intoxications (83.93%) and motor vehicular crashes or collisions (14.17%) that caused blunt traumas to the head and torso. More motor vehicular accidents were observed in CBs as a COD (n=52) than SCs (n=2). A total of four decedents died from drowning under the influence of CBs (n=2) and SCs (n=2). The natural cause (meaning from natural illnesses) was not directly identified as a cause of death among decedents with CBs and SCs as a COD. The reasons identified for those deaths that resulted in homicide (0.78%) were physical altercations with restraint and complications of restraint. There was no clear description of suicide (0.52%) on the FDLE report.

### Trends

A general linear model with repeated measures was used to examine the trends of cannabinoid death rate and synthetic cannabinoid death rate as a COD by Florida counties and by data years (2014–2020). For the trends of cannabinoid death rate, Mauchly’s test indicated that the assumption of sphericity was violated, X2(20) = 505.467, p <.001; therefore, Greenhouse-Geisser corrected tests were reported (ε= .293). Results indicated that there was no trend in cannabinoid death rate from 2014 to 2020, F(1.758, 114.276) = 1.739, p =.18, n2= .026. Specifically, there was no statistically significant linear trend in cannabinoid death rate, F(1, 65) = 2.290, p= .13, MSe = .547. Also, no statistically significant quadratic trend was noted, F(1, 65) = 1.794, p=.18, MSe = .092. Interestingly, there were no deaths from CBs in the rural or nonmetropolitan counties in Florida (n=23), only in urban or metropolitan counties (n=44).

Meanwhile, we also examined synthetic cannabinoid death rates from 2014 to 2020. The Mauchly test indicated that the assumption of sphericity was violated, X2(20) = 443.736, p <.001; therefore, the Greenhouse-Geisser tests were reported (ε=.397). There was a statistically significant trends in synthetic cannabinoid death rate in Florida from 2014 to 2020, F(2.383, 154.915) = 15.261, p <.001, MSe = 20.524. Specifically, data suggested a statistically significant linear trend in synthetic cannabinoid death rate, F(1, 65)= 29.887, p< .001, MSe = 7.226. There was also a statistically significant quadratic trend in synthetic cannabinoid death rate, F(1, 65) =18.537, p<.001, MSe= 6.443; and a statistically significant cubic trend in synthetic cannabinoid death rate, F(1, 65)= 19.946, p<.001, MSe= 8.018. Plots showing the temporal trends in CBs and SCs death rates are provided in figures 1 and 2.

## Discussion

This study examined the sociodemographic characteristics of decedents who died with CBs and SCs as a COD in Florida, the health-related conditions, the presence of other substances, and the manner of death associated with CBs and SCs as a COD from 2014 to 2020. Further, it examined the trends of death rates from these substances as a COD. There were a few studies available regarding CBs and SCs deaths. For instance, Hvozdovich and colleagues (2020) reported 54 cases of Florida prisoners who died from SCs between 2017 to 2018, analyzing the analytes of SC compounds identified in the prisoner’s blood and urine samples. Hvozdovich and colleagues (2020) did not report the death circumstances of these prisoners nor the health-related illnesses. While several studies on cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids focused on systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Whiting et al., 2015; Drummer, Gerostamoulos, & Woodford, 2019; Alves et al., 2020; Biasutti, Leffers, & Callaghan, 2020, and Hasin & Walsh, 2021), to our knowledge, this study is the first to conduct a multi-year analysis of CBs and SCs as a COD in a statewide level, including their death circumstances.

Our study results indicated that more males died from CBs and SCs than females; these results were congruent with other studies (Darke et al. 2020; Riederer et al., 2016). Darke et al. (2020) reported that 91.1% (n= 55) of people with synthetic cannabinoid-related deaths in Australia were male. It is noteworthy to mention that in the Darke et al. (2020) study, the number of deaths from SCs was 55, and it included 17 years of data in Australia (2000–2017). Our study included seven years of data (2014–2020), and the number of deaths reported from SCs as a COD was 258, which suggests a substantial increase in SCs mortality in different demographics. In addition, the results of our study indicated that non-Hispanic whites were more affected than any other race/ethnicity. Since available published studies on SCs as a COD are scarce, it is difficult to compare whether this result follows a similar pattern or not. Darke et al. (2020) and Trecki and colleagues (2015) did not include ethnicity or race in their study. Most studies on SCs as a COD were case studies (Adamowicz, Meissner & Maslanka, 2019; Angerer et al., 2017; Gerostamoulos, Drummer, & Woodford, 2015; Heath, Burroughs, Thompson, & Tecklenburg, 2012).

Meanwhile, the odds of reporting cannabis use were higher in young participants (50–64 years old) than those ≥ 65 years [1.00 vs 0.26, 95% CI 0.20, 0.34] (Hasin & Walsh, 2021), and 62% of cannabis-related deaths occurred in people under the age of forty (Zahra, Darke, Degenhardt, & Campbell, 2020). Our results concurred that people thirty-four years of age and below had nearly 54% deaths from CBs as a COD, specifically among 25–34 years of age at 32.8%. Moreover, our study results indicated that people ages 45–54 had the most SCs as a COD at 32.6 %, followed by 25–34 years at 18.6%, and 18–24 years at 5%. This result was different from what Trecki, Gerona, & Schwartz (2015) reported regarding synthetic cannabinoid-related illnesses and deaths, and that more deaths from SCs (n=7) occurred among 13–19 years old compared to those 40–49 years old (n=3) and 50–56 years old (n=2) in the U.S. from 2011–2015. The overall results of our study indicated that deaths from CBs and SCs were more prevalent in 45–54 years at nearly 28% than in the 18–24 years at 9.3%, suggesting a change in the age demographic in the context of mortality considering the attributable health conditions such as cardiovascular heart diseases. One possible explanation could be the difference in study years and location.

Over 13% of cases (52 out of 386 combined CBs and SCs as a COD) had cardiac-related conditions such as hypertensive heart disease, atherosclerotic and arteriosclerotic heart diseases, cardiac arrhythmias, and cardiomegaly. Pacher et al. (2018) explained that activating the CB1 receptors by the endocannabinoids and synthetic ligands might contribute to the cardiovascular disease process. Jouanjus, Raymond, Lapeyre-Mestre & Wolfe (2017) conducted a systematic review regarding cardiovascular risks in people who used cannabis and suggested more robust evidence of ischemic stroke, with less evidence on myocardial infarctions. Our study found one case of ischemic stroke with SCs as a COD, and one case of hemorrhagic stroke, also with SCs. Consequently, pulmonary-related conditions were also associated with both CBs and SCs as a COD, with three cases each for hypoxic encephalopathy, one case each for cardiorespiratory failure and bronchopneumonia. Zawatzky, Abdalla, & Cinar (2020) reported that SCs use could induce alveolar inflammation through the activation of CB1 receptors, which in turn could explain this study’s findings of the presence of bronchopneumonia (n=1), emphysema (n=1), and acute respiratory episode (n=1) among the cases of SCs as a COD.

There are also essential findings from this study that were closely congruent with previous studies, such as accident-related deaths from CBs and SCs. For instance, Darke et al. (2019) reported that 47.3% (26 out of 55) of synthetic cannabinoid-related deaths in Australia died from accidental drug toxicity from 2000 to 2017, whereas, in our study, nearly 99% of decedents suffered from accidental drug intoxications. Also, Riederer et al. (2016) reported 456 cases of SC intoxications in the US from 2010 to 2015, where 61% of the cases had SCs as the only drug involved. In our study, there were 258 cases of SCs as a COD from 2014 to 2020, with nearly 65% of cases involving SCs as the only drug involved. Although the timeframe of our study was different from that of Riederer and colleagues (2016), the number of deaths from SCs is concerning given that our study only examined SCs as a COD in Florida and that the number of SCs as a COD was more than half of the SCs deaths reported by Riederer et al. (2016) nationwide. Additionally, Hvozdovich, Chronister, Logan & Goldberger (2020) reported 54 cases of Florida prisoners with SCs deaths from 2017 to 2018, with 5F- ADB (96.3%) being the most detected SC chemical compound through blood and urine samples. Our study identified 5F- ADB as the most prevalent SC chemical compound at nearly 26% (n=67). It should be noted that Hvozdovich and colleagues (2020) did not include the manner of death of prisoners who died from SCs.

Meanwhile, for the trends of cannabis death rate, only SCs death rate indicated statistically significant linear and quadratic trends from 2014 to 2020 in Florida. Comparatively, little research has been done about the trends on CBs and SCs as a COD. Most studies on these CB or SC trends focused on cannabis use (Hasin & Walsh, 2021; Ta, Greto & Bolt, 2019). More research on cannabis-related mortality is warranted.

Deaths resulting from motor vehicular collisions while under the influence of cannabis are well-documented. Els et al. (2019) reported that the presence of cannabis increased the odds of road traffic collisions (OR 2.49, 95% CI 1.68–3.71, p<.00001, n=49,870. Hall (2015) reported that research over the past twenty years has revealed that driving under the influence of cannabis doubled the risks of motor vehicle collisions. In a meta-analysis on cannabis use and vehicular motor crashes, Li et al. (2012) reported that drivers who tested positive for cannabis use and those who self-reported to have used cannabis were twice as likely to be involved in vehicular motor crashes than non-cannabis users. Meanwhile, Bondallaz et al. (2016) reported that cannabis affected actual driving performance, as evidenced by drivers under the influence of cannabis increased lane weaving or the distance headway to the preceding vehicle. Aston and colleagues (2016) reported that perceptions that driving under the influence of cannabis is less dangerous than driving under the influence of alcohol were linked to an increased likelihood of driving after smoking cannabis, contributing to an increased risk of VMA. Our study results indicated that more motor vehicle accidents occurred in decedents with CBs as a COD (n=52) than SCs (n=2). It is noteworthy that cannabis remains in the body system for days or weeks after the last use (Cochrane, 2022; NIDA, 2021c), though its intoxicating and impairing effects dissipate after hours.

The findings of this study are subject to some limitations. First, no inferences are made to the co-use of other substances such as methamphetamine, amphetamine, heroin, cocaine, opiates such as fentanyl, oxycodone, or ethanol to either CBs or SCs since the strengths of these drugs are not readily available. (There were only 2 cases of ethanol where BAC results were available on the FDLE reports). The same is valid with the CBs and SCs, where the THC levels, to the most degree, were not available on the FDLE reports. Another limitation of this study is that we identified the associated health-related conditions listed under the cause of death in the FDLE reports with no inferences about the severity of these health-related conditions and their contributory or causal effects on CBs and SCs a COD. The demographics in Florida counties might differ from other counties or settings; hence no generalizability of results is implied.

### Clinical Implications

The results of this study have clinical or healthcare implications. Understandably, as the public and scientific interests in cannabis and cannabis-related products are mounting, and more states in the U.S. are legalizing the medical and recreational use of cannabis, the public is warned about the unsubstantiated claims regarding cannabis-related products in treating health-related conditions. For instance, FDA (2020b) cautioned the public about the health benefit claims about CBD (which is often associated with cannabis), such as reduction in pain, anxiety, and enhanced sleep. Research on these medical benefits is underway (NIDA, 2019), but it is early to confirm their safety. Cannabis remains to have a potential addictive effect (NIDA, 2021b; Keyhani et al., 2018; Volkow, Baler, Compton & Weiss, 2014).

The adverse effects of CBs and SCs are well-documented to include physiologic symptoms such as tachypnea, tachycardia, high blood pressure, intense nausea and vomiting, chest pain, heart attack, rhabdomyolysis, kidney problem, and death (CDC, 2018). Also, CDC (2018) reported the clinical manifestations of synthetic cannabinoid poisonings such as agitation, sleepiness, irritability, confusion, dizziness, incoordination, inability to concentrate, stroke, and seizure. SC intoxications’ psychiatric signs and symptoms include hallucinations, delusions, psychosis, violent behavior, and suicidal thoughts (CDC, 2018). Withdrawal symptoms from heavy use of SCs include headache, nausea, vomiting, severe anxiety, sweating, trouble sleeping, breathing problems, chest pain, palpitations, tachycardia, and seizures (CDC, 2018).

Since some people believe that synthetic cannabinoids could not be easily detected in the urine, thus increasing the propensity of CBs or SCs use. As newer SC compounds are continually emerging, detecting SC in the urine is pretty challenging, particularly in routine urine drug testing (Castaneto et al., 2015). CDC (2018) acknowledged the challenges in diagnosing synthetic cannabinoid-related illnesses (SCRI), either through laboratory methods or clinical manifestations. CDC (2018) recommended considering SCRI in patients with altered mental status without other obvious explanation; and that most hospital drug screens could not detect the presence of SCs. Some studies reported the use of some techniques in detecting SCs. For instance, Adamowicz, Meissner, & Maslanka (2019) reported screening SC AMB-FUBINACA and EMB-FIMNACA with high-performance liquid chromatography with diode array detection (HPLC-DAD), liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Castaneto et al. (2015) used the comprehensive urine quantitative LC-MS/MS method in detecting 22 metabolites from SC compounds.

As of this writing, the Food and Drug Administration approved a few medications that contain dronabinol (a synthetic THC)—Marinol and Syndros, and Cesamet (which contains nabilone- a synthetic substance similar to THC) for the treatment of weight loss and anorexia in people with HIV/AIDS (NCCIH, 2019). Nabilone is the only synthetic cannabinoid with medical usage, and it is used to treat nausea associated with cancer chemotherapy (EMCDDA, n.d.). So far, there is only one CBD product approved by the FDA, a prescription drug used to treat seizures in people one year and older, such as seizures from Lennox Gastaut Syndrome, Dravet Syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis complex (FDA, 2020). Unfortunately, there is no FDA-approved drug that acts as an antidote for synthetic cannabinoids toxicity (CDC, 2018). According to NIDA (2021), behavioral therapies and medications had not been clinically assessed to treat SC products-related addiction. However, CDC (2018) recommended supportive treatment such as intravenous (IV) fluids, supplemental oxygen, airway protection, anti-emetic agents, and IV benzodiazepines for agitation, combativeness, and hyperactivity in patients with SCRIs.

## Conclusions

The persistent deaths from cannabinoids and synthetic cannabinoids are a legitimate public health concern. Males are disproportionately affected than females. Our study showed that more deaths happened among 45–54 years of age, particularly with SCs, which could translate to potential work safety issues. Also, our study indicated that drug intoxications and motor vehicle collisions are adverse outcomes of CBs and SCs, either used singly or in combination with other drugs. These findings call for strategic interventions to reduce avoidable deaths from these substances. While CBs as a COD was primarily concentrated in urban counties, many SCs deaths happened in rural or nonmetropolitan counties. The statistically significant linear and quadratic trends in synthetic cannabinoid death rates warrant continuous monitoring and surveillance. Despite government health warnings about the harms and danger of SCs, and that SCs are not for human consumption, unfortunately, there are a number of people who suffer from acute SC intoxications and deaths. The public should remain vigilant of the adverse health outcomes associated with using CBs and SCs and the unpredictable effects of these substances, particularly with people who have underlying cardiovascular-related illnesses.
